scopes.Noach: Selected Breslov teachings on Parshas Noach. Alternative readings are noted beside the affected passages.
scopes.Lech: Selected teachings and printed notes from pages 77–109, not the whole portion anthology or book. Wording, vocalization and citations remain uncertain where qualified beside the passages.

notes.readerText: “Offered up his life” means self-sacrifice for Israel; this clause does not say Moshe died in doing so.
The readings are uncertain: אֲמָרִית / אָמָרִית and עַלְוָון / עַלְוָן / עַלְוֹן.
The reading is uncertain: בְּעַיִּל / בְּעַיִּיל / בְּעַיִל.
בְּגָבְהָהּ / בְּגֹבְהָהּ / בְּגוֹבְהָהּ means “its height”; the spelling and vocalization are uncertain. The readings וַתָּנַח / וַתַּנַח and תִּשְׁרִי / תִשְׁרִי are also uncertain.
The first and second occurrences are each uncertain between ׳עַיִּל׳ / ׳עַיִּיל׳ / ׳עַיִל׳; neither occurrence settles the other.
The vocalizations are uncertain: הֵיצֵא / הֵיצֶא and בְּעַל / בַּעַל.
The vocalization of this occurrence is uncertain: עַיִּל / עַיִל.
The vocalization is uncertain: מְזֻמָּן / מְזֻמָן. The meaning is “ready.”
קש״ת is a mnemonic for three shofar sounds; their English names do not convey this Hebrew wordplay. The excerpt refers back to three points earlier in its source.
יַמְשִׁיךְ (“will draw down”) has no named subject: context may mean God acting through the righteous person, or the righteous person.
These occurrences have uncertain readings: בְּעַיִּל / בְּעַיִּיל / בְּעַיִל, אַפְתְּחַת / אַפְתְחַת and תַּרְעִין / תַרְעִין.
The printed citation is Laws of Shabbos, Halacha 4, item 69; the matching passage in the comparison text is Halacha 7, items 69–71.
“The aforementioned hidden kindness” refers to material earlier in the cited source, before this excerpt.
In “according to his power and will he sustains the world,” context points to the righteous person; vowel pointing alone does not settle the pronoun.
“Before Him” contextually means God. שֶׁנִּתַּן means “permission was given”; its passive clause does not name the giver, and pointing alone does not establish the divine referent.
The printed citation is Laws of Circumcision, Halacha 3, item 4; the matching comparison passage begins item 7.
“Flood/confusion” expresses the Hebrew wordplay מַבּוּל/בִּלְבּוּל. The parenthetical conversation is the source’s own report.
מָעֳמָד / מָעָמָד are alternatives: the ayin vowel is uncertain between hataf-kamatz and kamatz. The meaning is no standing place.
מַיִם׳ / מָיִם׳ are alternatives in the first depths-water quotation; the mem vowel is uncertain between patach and kamatz.
This occurrence of נִתְגַּלֶּה / נִתְגַּלָּה has an uncertain lamed vowel between segol and kamatz; the meaning is revelation.
The second occurrence is also uncertain between נִתְגַּלֶּה / נִתְגַּלָּה. This uncertainty does not apply to the earlier שנתגלה or the final-paragraph נתגלה.
No particular main teaching is identified for this printed note.
“[How could I]” is context supplied in English. וכ״ש שאתפלל על אחרים literally means “and all the more so that I should pray for others.”
ועבור לתחתונים על רצונך has no explicit word for offenses; “[by overlooking their offenses]” expresses the contextual sense.
למקומך reads “until you reach your place,” differing from the familiar maxim’s “his place.”
This note relates to the self-judgment teaching through its item 282 reference and subject matter; an explicit printed link is not established.
פ"מ (P.M.) is an unresolved acronym.
חִדּוּשׁ הָעוֹלָם means the world’s coming into being, not eternity; the passage is polemical.
אֲחָדִים means common words in the verse; חַדִּים means sharp words in its interpretation.
The initial-he vowel of הֻכְרַח is uncertain. The clause describes compulsion to come forth from Terach, without naming another acting subject.
כַּמָּה גִּלְגּוּלִין means many turnings—the divine circuitous means described by the events here—not necessarily multiple individual lifetimes.
היכלי התמורות and סטרא אחרא are technical chambers of exchanges and the Other Side.
מעש is a defective, unpointed noun amid the surrounding pointed text.
This note relates by its Likutay Torah on Iyov reference and subject matter to the captured-souls teaching; an explicit printed link is not established.
ע"י. ends the first nourishment clause without a following noun or pronoun. ‘[It]’ is supplied from the immediately repeated explanation that they are nourished through the soul.
ומצא has no expressed subject in this excerpt; “[he]” leaves the agent unspecified.
כי כיון (“for, since”) begins an irregular final clause that stops at במקום המטונף כזה (“in such a filthy place”).
Amatlai is a possible conventional rendering of unpointed אמתלאי; its vowels are uncertain.
Charan (חרן) is linked with wrath (חרון אף).
The lamed/yud vocalization of דְּאִתְגַּלְי' is uncertain in this occurrence.
This is the portion heading, not another teaching. The Hebrew heading has no vowel points.
Quotation marks represent the shapes in the print; their original character encoding is unknown.
Rabbainu means ‘our teacher’; this sentence does not give a personal name.
‘The above’ and ‘above’ refer to the argument within this text.
Quotation marks represent the printed shapes; their original character encoding is unknown.
The singular ‘soul’ is followed by the masculine הוא (‘is’).
Note 56 concerns this birth discussion. Its ‘there’ refers back to the section 14 reference, after which the raised נו appears.
The statements about conception, inherited desire, parental thoughts and impossibility of reversal are claims of the cited source; they do not by themselves establish a scientific account.
The wording shifts from plural ‘them’ to singular ‘his father’; the feminine form of ‘the essential’ refers to the soul.
‘[element]’ supplies an understood predicate in ‘the soul, which is the essential [element] in the person’; no corresponding noun appears in the Hebrew.
The singular pronouns follow a compound list. ‘He’ refers to the strengthening antagonist and ‘one’ to the person resisting him; no particular human antagonist is named.
Quotation marks represent the printed shapes; their original character encoding is unknown.
נפשותינו משרשת has a plural noun, ‘our souls,’ with a singular feminine participle.

The consonants שמגדל concern upbringing. שֶׁמְּגַדֵּל and שֶׁמְּגֻדָּל are possible readings: the vowel clusters beneath gimel and dalet are uncertain, and the displayed points are provisional. No additional acting subject is identified.
The word is provisionally שמרמזת, possibly שמרומזת with a thin ו after ר. ‘Alluding’ leaves these consonantal alternatives open. The reference is to Yeshaya chapter 31.
ומה שירדה עליו שלותו and וכשם שהם היה קשה עליהם משא הדרך have difficult syntax in this quotation.
The outbreak term is provisionally עֲפִישׁ, possibly עֲפוּשׁ, with uncertain interior letter and vowels. The parallel wording עפוש suggests ‘pestilence,’ which remains a provisional meaning here.
The printed citation gives item 74; the electronic parallel is headed item 75. These are different numbering references.
The available electronic Redemption of the Firstborn record does not contain this quotation. The printed cross-references to other texts remain independently unconfirmed.
The vowel points are provisional. Tiny marks and the original character encoding remain uncertain.
The summary says ‘the suppressed evil’; the introduction and body say ‘the suppressed good.’ These are different readings.
This clause says ‘the altar is perfected’; the earlier introduction says ‘the imaginative faculty is perfected.’

This is the compiler’s shorter excerpt, with one cry of ‘gevald’ and an unpointed Rashi abbreviation. The electronic edition is longer. Vowel points are provisional; tiny marks and original character encoding remain uncertain.

This note concerns the young-and-old passage. ‘Stopped up from above’ is opaque wording. The electronic Shabbos 7, item 8 passage is different. The note-marker shape and original character encoding are uncertain.

This note concerns the ‘thousands of books’ passage and continues onto the next page. Its Bris Menuchah quotation has no independent underlying witness here. מגישים (‘present at’) and the parenthesized מביטים (‘look toward’) are separate readings concerning the princes and his table. The note-marker shape and original character encoding are uncertain.

This note concerns the Yaakov-books passage. The Rosh Chodesh and Likutay Moharan quotations have the limits shown here; the concluding Parparaos LaChochmah narrative has only this printed witness. The note-marker shape and original character encoding are uncertain.
מוהר״ר is an honorific; no personal name is given here.

The closing citation gives Rosh Chodesh, Halacha 6, item 45; the electronic parallel and note 65 give Halacha 7, item 45. Vowel points are provisional; tiny marks and original character encoding remain uncertain.
‘Sparks that fell from the depths of the shells’ is this passage’s wording. The Hebrew parallels differ in extent. Vowel points, tiny marks and original character encoding remain uncertain.
The term bazak denotes a flashing appearance; the teaching connects it with broken earthenware and the fire between the shards.

This note concerns the Ari-writings reference after the Adam-and-sparks passage and continues onto the next page. Its Likutay Torah and Chariots of Truth quotations have no independent underlying witnesses here. מהר״א מששון is an abbreviated author designation. The raised-marker shape and original character encoding are uncertain.

This note concerns renewed repair of the worlds and vessels. Its Aitz Chayim, gate 18 quotation has no independent underlying witness here. The raised-marker shape and original character encoding are uncertain.

This note concerns sparks remaining unrefined before Moshiach. Its three Aitz Chayim quotations have no independent underlying witness here. The raised-marker shape and original character encoding are uncertain.

The citation gives Nefilas Apayim, Halacha 6; Hebrew parallels differ in wording and extent. Vowel points are provisional, including the vowel cluster in זֻהֲמַת (‘contamination’) in the Esther paragraph. Tiny marks and original character encoding remain uncertain.
This one-sentence note links Sarah’s taking with the preceding discussion of Abraham’s trial. The raised-marker shape and original character encoding are uncertain.

The citation gives Tefillin, Halacha 6, item 27. The electronic Hebrew parallel’s Chronicles reference differs from the printed chapter 36. Vowel points are provisional, including the separate זֻהֲמַת (‘contamination’) occurrence in the other-side paragraph. Tiny marks and original character encoding remain uncertain. Note 70 has no assigned main teaching.

This note’s backward reference follows the discussion of Moshe and Israel bringing Israel out of Pharaoh’s domain; its target is not named here. The raised-marker shape and original character encoding are uncertain.

The teaching begins with its verse, without a separate summary. Note 72 concerns this teaching by context, though the raised marker’s identity remains uncertain. Tiny marks and original character encoding also remain uncertain. Its assertions are those of the source.

Note 72 concerns the first teaching on page 99 by context. The quotations and underlying teaching have only this printed-note witness here, not separate originals. The raised marker’s identity, tiny marks and original character encoding remain uncertain.

A separate compiler’s aside accompanies this discussion. Notes 73 and 74 concern the teaching by context; their raised markers remain uncertain. The printed quotations and difficult forms remain distinct from the larger parallels rather than settled by standard biblical wording. Some words have no vowel points. Tiny marks and original character encoding remain uncertain. The assertions are those of the source.
The Yiddish designation אָן זֶעצִירְס is retained literally; no English expansion is supplied.
The internal tav dot is uncertain: שִׁתִי and שִׁתִּי are possible readings.
בְּתֹקֶף, without a vav, is an intensity noun, not ‘was repaired.’ The clause concerns finding good within the intensity of the bad days’ prevailing.

This small-font compiler parenthesis crosses pages 99–100. It concerns the surrounding discussion but is a separate aside, not another teaching or numbered note. Tiny marks and original character encoding remain uncertain; its logical grouping differs from the page sequence.

The printed sequence is the first body paragraph, the first aside half, note 72 in the page 99 footer, the page break, then the second aside half and second body paragraph. Thus note 72 lies physically between the aside halves, although it concerns the first teaching on page 99 by context. Raised-marker identity remains uncertain.

Note 73 concerns the second teaching beginning on page 99 by context. The underlying teaching has no separate witness here. Raised-marker identity, tiny marks and original character encoding are uncertain.

Note 74 concerns the second teaching beginning on page 99 by context. The underlying commentary has no separate witness here. Raised-marker identity, tiny marks and original character encoding are uncertain.

This block begins with its verse, without a separate summary. רש״י has no vowel points here. The electronic Hebrew parallels are larger and have textual defects; they do not settle the printed excerpt’s wording or extent. Tiny marks and original character encoding remain uncertain. Its assertions are those of the source.

The passage continues across pages 103–104. שם/שם, the abbreviated quotation ending וכולי and the unpointed רש״י belong to this excerpt. The internal reference is (כמובא בסימן ד׳ לקוטי חלק א), with לקוטי. Electronic parallels are larger; their locators and pointing do not settle these printed references or marks. Tiny marks and original character encoding remain uncertain. Its assertions are those of the source.

This upper block precedes the lower teaching. The compound concerning Dovid, Messiah and the root of the good point has anomalous wording, explained beside its clause. Larger Hebrew parallels repeat or vary clauses. Tiny marks and original character encoding remain uncertain. Its assertions are those of the source.
שֶׁהוּא וְשֹׁרֶשׁ literally reads ‘who is and root.’ The second ‘[is]’ supplies English syntax; the anomalous conjunction remains unresolved.

כעת חיה is interpreted here as ‘at this living time.’ The two birth-noun occurrences have separately provisional points. The printed Circumcision 4, item 16 citation differs from the Gairim 3 parallel; textual correspondence does not settle the citation. Tiny marks and original character encoding remain uncertain. Its assertions are those of the source.
The birth noun has the consonants הולדת. הוֹלַדְת has provisional vowels and no tav dagesh here. The unpointed הולדת states the consonants alone, not a settled alternative vocalization.
The later birth-noun occurrence הוֹלַדְתּוֹ has independently uncertain vowels and tav dot; the earlier occurrence does not settle it.
The citation is (הלכות מילה הלכה ד׳ אות ט״ז), Circumcision 4, item 16. The textual parallel is under Gairim, Halacha 3, a different reference; the citation’s authority remains unresolved.

The compiler’s introduction and Likutay Moharan II reference are separate from the quoted body. The opening על פי is unpointed. Electronic item 9 offers introductory context and items 10–11 body parallels, not identical excerpt limits. The printed reference is Partners in Land 5. Tiny marks and original character encoding remain uncertain. Its assertions are those of the source.
The opening על פי has no vowel points here; עַל פִּי is not an established printed vocalization of this occurrence.

תמימות means wholehearted simplicity, in contrast to divination or forceful cleverness. The printed reference is Damages 5, item 16; the larger electronic parallel is item 15. Tiny marks and original character encoding remain uncertain. Its assertions are those of the source.

Note 75 concerns the concealed-Torah reference by context and appears in the page 108 footer, before the page 109 continuation. Its main-text reference is not another note body. The two seven-token yud-dot uncertainties are independent. The Hebrew parallels are larger than this excerpt, which ends with Circumcision 3. Raised-marker identity, tiny marks and original character encoding remain uncertain. Its assertions are those of the source.
In this first seven-token occurrence the yud dot is uncertain: בְּזַיִ״ן or בְּזַיִּ״ן.
In this second seven-token occurrence the yud dot is independently uncertain: הַזַּיִ״ן or הַזַּיִּ״ן.

Note 75 includes ‘gratuitous kindness’ and Likutay Moharan II, item 78. It concerns the main passage’s concealed-Torah reference by context, but its complete body has no independent underlying witness here. Raised-marker identity, tiny marks and original character encoding remain uncertain. Its assertion is that of the source.
The raised marker נט is unestablished; this note has no assigned main teaching.
The raised marker ס is unestablished; this note has no assigned main teaching.
והסתיר את עצמו כל המדריגות לפני הסט״א has no linking preposition before ‘all the levels.’ ‘[at]’ supplies a minimal English link; the intended construction remains uncertain.

This independent note continues across pages 96–97 and includes two Zohar quotations, a Likutay Moharan quotation and an Or HaTorah quotation ending with the Mikaitz parenthesis. The cited Zohar is 82a/b, not the electronic 81b comparison; those Zohar and Or HaTorah passages have no independent corresponding witness here. The Moharan 62 quotation has ‘beauty of the splendor and majesty of the glory’; the parallel differs in wording concerning speech and in excerpt extent. Tiny marks and original character encoding remain uncertain.
This note has no established main-text marker or assigned main teaching. Proximity and subject matter do not give it an owner.
